issues.legal_issue: Continuity of a state of things may be inferred retrospectively only when the earlier period is reasonably proximate in light of the nature of the thing and surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: Later survey records showed that the claimants’ ancestors held some frontier plots during 1892 to 1909.
The claimed accretions formed during 1845 to 1863, leaving a considerable gap between the recorded state of affairs and the period for which continuity was asserted.
Ownership of some plots had changed even during the later period, and frontier plots and corresponding accretions were not always held by the same persons.
The frontier lands were subject to inundation, and char-land settlements were seasonal and temporary.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to infer that the ancestors held the frontier plots during the period when the accretions formed, because the long gap and surrounding circumstances made that inference unsafe.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, an existing state of things may support an inference of continuity forwards and, in appropriate cases, backwards. The presumption weakens with the passage of time, and its reach depends on the nature of the thing and the surrounding circumstances. The Court approved Anangamanjari Chowdhrani v. Tripura Sundari Chowdhrani and referred to Bristow v. Cormican and Deo v. Young; it disapproved contrary observations in Manmath Nath Haldar v. Girish Chandra Roy and Hemendra Nath Roy Chowdhury v. Jnendra Prasanna Bhaduri.

rule.if: civil_property_title_dispute and later_state_of_things_proved and earlier_period_distant and intervening_conditions_unstable

predicates.civil_property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to title in property.
predicates.later_state_of_things_proved: Evidence establishes a state of things at a later time.
predicates.earlier_period_distant: The period for which continuity is asserted is substantially earlier than the proved state of things.
predicates.intervening_conditions_unstable: The evidence shows changes in ownership or other circumstances making the state of things liable to change over time.

issues.definition: When a property dispute relies on a later-proved state of things to establish an earlier one, a distant earlier period and unstable intervening conditions mean continuity is not inferred retrospectively.

issues.legal_issue: A decision in earlier litigation concerning different property does not operate as res judicata in a later property dispute.
material_facts: The claimants relied on decisions in earlier suits to support their title to the lands in dispute.
Those earlier suits did not concern any portion of the property involved in the present suit.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decisions did not operate as res judicata in the present suit.
issues.legal_principle: The principle of res judicata does not make a decision conclusive in a later suit concerning property that was not the subject matter of the earlier litigation.

predicates.civil_property_title_suit: The proceeding is a suit concerning title to property.
predicates.earlier_decision_relied_on: A party relies on a decision made in earlier litigation.
predicates.earlier_decision_concerns_different_prop: The property at issue in the earlier litigation is different from the property in the current suit.

issues.definition: In a property-title suit, an earlier decision about different property does not determine the current dispute as res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: An entry showing a tenancy at a fixed rent does not, by itself, establish that the tenancy existed from the time of the Permanent Settlement.
material_facts: A record of rights described certain tenancies as being at a fixed rate of rent.
The claimants argued that the entry, read with section 50(2) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, showed that their ancestors held the plots from the time of the Permanent Settlement.
The circumstances in which the entries were made and whether they concerned the relevant frontier plots had not been investigated.
The point was not raised in the courts below and was raised for the first time at the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The fixed-rent entries did not establish that the tenancies dated from the Permanent Settlement, and the Court declined to allow the newly raised point to be argued without the relevant circumstances having been investigated.
issues.legal_principle: Section 50(2) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, provides a presumption, in a suit or proceeding under that Act, that a raiyat has held at the same rate of rent since the Permanent Settlement if the rate has not changed during the preceding twenty years. Fixity of rent may also result from an express grant, so an entry recording a fixed rate does not necessarily establish the historical commencement of the tenancy. A new point dependent on uninvestigated circumstances should not be allowed to be raised for the first time at the final appellate stage.

rule.if: civil_property_title_appeal and record_shows_fixed_rent and historical_duration_unproved and entry_circumstances_uninvestigated and argument_first_raised_on_final_appeal

predicates.civil_property_title_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a dispute over title to property.
predicates.record_shows_fixed_rent: A land record describes a tenancy as having a fixed rate of rent.
predicates.historical_duration_unproved: The evidence does not establish how long the tenancy or fixed rate had existed.
predicates.entry_circumstances_uninvestigated: The circumstances behind the record entry, or whether it concerns the relevant land, have not been investigated.
predicates.argument_first_raised_on_final_appeal: A party raises the argument for the first time in the final appeal.

issues.definition: In a property-title appeal, a fixed-rent entry with no proof of historical duration does not establish an ancient tenancy, and a first-time appellate argument dependent on uninvestigated circumstances is not considered.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking title to alluvial accretions must establish that the accretions attached to plots held by the claimant or the claimant’s predecessors and must identify the accretions attributable to those plots.
material_facts: The claimants relied on a statutory claim to lands said to have formed through river accretion.
The evidence did not establish that the claimants or their ancestors held the plots to which the disputed accretions were said to have attached when the accretions formed.
The evidence showed that different branches separately held and enjoyed frontier plots, and the claimants made no attempt in the courts below to apportion the accretions among the plots.
The claimants did not plead or prove joint ownership and possession with the other branch, and the evidence did not establish that the other branch had lost its title.
The claimants advanced a new theory of common ownership by a remote ancestor only at the Supreme Court, without supporting pleadings or proof.
issues.conclusion: The claimants failed to establish title to the disputed accretions or a right to recover the entire area. The Court stated that accretions must be apportioned by drawing perpendicular lines from the boundary points of each plot to the new river course, but declined to remand the case for the missing investigation. It did not express an opinion on whether the lands had been gained by gradual accession.
issues.legal_principle: Under clause (1) of section 4 of Bengal Alluvion and Deluvion Regulation XI of 1825, a claimant must prove gradual accession from the recess of the river and that the accretion attached to plots in the possession of the claimant or the claimant’s predecessors. The entitlement extends only to accretions before the relevant plots; where multiple plots are involved, their accretions must be apportioned by projecting perpendicular lines from their boundary points to the new river course. A claim to the whole area also requires pleading and proof of the asserted joint title and possession.

rule.if: alluvial_title_claim and claimant_plot_holding_at_accretion_unproved and separate_plot_holders_identified and accretions_not_apportioned

predicates.alluvial_title_claim: The proceeding includes a claim to title based on land formed by river accretion.
predicates.claimant_plot_holding_at_accretion_unpro: The claimant does not prove that the claimant or predecessors held the plots to which the claimed accretions attached when they formed.
predicates.separate_plot_holders_identified: The evidence indicates that different persons or branches separately held the relevant frontier plots.
predicates.accretions_not_apportioned: The claimant does not identify or establish which accretions belong to the plots held by the claimant’s predecessors.

issues.definition: A claimant who cannot prove relevant plot holding at the time of accretion and does not apportion accretions among separately held plots cannot establish a right to the entire accreted area.

issues.legal_issue: A title claim cannot be established by an unproved oral arrangement, an unsupported assertion of occupancy, or a mere admission that does not itself transfer title.
material_facts: The claimants alleged occupancy rights over a much larger area than the survey records attributed to their branch; the survey evidence recorded only about nineteen bighas for that branch.
The alleged oral arrangement with the landholder was not established.
The evidence of possession before 1909 was not convincing, and the Court had found that the claimants and their ancestors were not in possession of the disputed land since 1909.
An admission about tenancy rights was made in circumstances the Court regarded as suspicious, was not followed by a formal amendment to the written statement, and had weak evidentiary value.
The claimants did not claim tenancy rights by express grant or adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The claimants failed to prove title through the alleged occupancy, oral arrangement, or possession. The admission did not establish title, and mere occupation did not confer tenancy rights.
issues.legal_principle: Title must be established by legally sufficient proof; it does not pass merely by admission. An admission may have weak evidentiary value in the circumstances in which it was made, and mere occupation does not by itself confer tenancy rights.

rule.if: civil_property_title_claim and (oral_arrangement_unproved or occupancy_evidence_insufficient or admission_only_supports_title or possession_is_only_basis)

predicates.civil_property_title_claim: A party seeks a declaration or recovery of property on the basis of title.
predicates.oral_arrangement_unproved: The party relies on an alleged oral arrangement that is not proved.
predicates.occupancy_evidence_insufficient: The records and other evidence do not establish the claimed occupancy rights.
predicates.admission_only_supports_title: The party relies on an admission that does not independently establish or transfer title.
predicates.possession_is_only_basis: The party relies on occupation alone without establishing a legal basis for tenancy or ownership.

issues.definition: In a property-title claim, an unproved arrangement, insufficient occupancy evidence, an admission alone, or mere occupation does not establish title.

issues.legal_issue: Testimony from earlier litigation is admissible against another party only if the statutory conditions for its use are satisfied, while a party’s own admission is evidence against that party.
material_facts: The claimants relied on depositions from witnesses in earlier litigation.
The deposition of one defendant was treated as an admission against that defendant but not against the other defendants.
The other earlier depositions did not satisfy the requirements for admissibility under section 33 of the Indian Evidence Act.
issues.conclusion: The deposition that constituted an admission was admissible against its maker but not the other defendants, and the other prior depositions were inadmissible because they did not satisfy section 33.
issues.legal_principle: Section 33 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, governs the admissibility of testimony from an earlier proceeding. An admission is evidence against its maker but is not, on that basis alone, admissible against other parties.

rule.if: civil_property_title_dispute and prior_proceeding_testimony_relied_on and (statutory_conditions_for_prior_testimony_unmet or admission_made_by_different_party)

predicates.civil_property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to title in property.
predicates.prior_proceeding_testimony_relied_on: A party relies on testimony given in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.statutory_conditions_for_prior_testimony: The conditions required for using testimony from the earlier proceeding are not satisfied.
predicates.admission_made_by_different_party: The asserted admission was made by a party other than the person against whom it is offered.

issues.definition: In a property dispute, prior testimony that fails the conditions for reuse, or an admission made by someone else, is not admissible against the opposing parties.
